sum: From reveille at five in the morning to lights out, Alexander Solzhenitsyn follows a single day of Ivan Denisovich Shukhov, a peasant and former soldier serving ten years in a Soviet labour camp on false charges of spying. Through his small victories, an extra bowl of gruel, a well-laid wall, a hidden crust of bread, the novella reveals the brutality and the dignity of camp life.
bg: Solzhenitsyn, who had himself spent eight years in the camps, published the novella in 1962 in the journal Novy Mir with Nikita Khrushchev’s personal approval during a brief thaw in censorship. It caused a sensation as the first open Soviet account of the Gulag, and Solzhenitsyn won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1970.
br: Short and continuous, without chapter breaks; read it in one or two sittings to feel the length of the single day. Notice how much hangs on tiny details of food, warmth and work.
la: Solzhenitsyn writes in a close third person saturated with Shukhov’s peasant idiom and camp slang, so the reader experiences the day through his practical, unsentimental eyes, which makes the horror more powerful.
cx: The camps held millions under Stalin. Solzhenitsyn’s later three-volume The Gulag Archipelago documented the system in full and led to his expulsion from the Soviet Union in 1974.
th: Survival and dignity
Shukhov keeps his humanity through work, cunning and small kindnesses.
Injustice
Ordinary people were imprisoned on absurd charges by a vast system.
Work and meaning
Even forced labour can become a source of pride and self-respect.
fit: A short, powerful classic that adds twentieth-century Russian history to your classics shelf.
mis: Its unrelenting focus on a single grim day may feel narrow or bleak to some readers.
rq: What counts as a good day for Shukhov?
How does he keep his dignity?
What do the other prisoners reveal about the system?
dq: Why is the story told about one ordinary day rather than an extraordinary one?
What does the novella say about resistance?
rel: Dostoevsky, who also endured Siberian prison.

sum: On the day of his wedding, the young sailor Edmond Dantès is falsely accused of treason by jealous rivals and imprisoned without trial in the island fortress of the Château d’If. After years of despair, a fellow prisoner teaches him and reveals the location of a vast treasure. Dantès escapes, transforms himself into the mysterious Count of Monte Cristo, and sets out to reward his friends and punish his enemies.
bg: Alexandre Dumas published the novel as a newspaper serial from 1844 to 1846, written with his collaborator Auguste Maquet. It became one of the most popular novels ever written and has been adapted countless times. Dumas also wrote The Three Musketeers.
br: It is very long, so choose an unabridged modern translation, such as Robin Buss’s for Penguin, rather than older abridged versions. The prison section is gripping; the middle Paris section introduces many characters, so keep notes.
la: Dumas writes with theatrical flair: cliffhangers, disguises, secret identities and grand set pieces, all designed for serial readers waiting for the next instalment, with a vast cast whose fates interlock.
cx: The story spans the fall of Napoleon, the Bourbon restoration and the July Monarchy, and satirises the corruption of French society, banking, law and politics under the new bourgeois order.
th: Revenge and justice
Dantès wonders whether he is God’s instrument or merely vengeful.
Patience and hope
Wait and hope becomes the novel’s final lesson.
Identity and transformation
Dantès remakes himself completely to gain power over his enemies.
fit: A thrilling, page-turning classic that offers pure narrative pleasure among the weightier books on your list.
mis: Very long, with complicated subplots and coincidences that stretch belief. Patience through the middle is rewarded.
rq: When does justice turn into revenge for Dantès?
Which of his enemies is most interesting?
dq: What does wait and hope mean at the end?
rel: Hugo’s Notre-Dame, another French Romantic epic.

sum: In medieval Paris of 1482, the beautiful Roma dancer Esmeralda captivates three men: the tormented archdeacon Claude Frollo, the shallow captain Phoebus, and the deaf bell-ringer Quasimodo, who lives hidden in the towers of Notre-Dame cathedral. Their obsessions lead to accusation, trial and tragedy, while the cathedral itself looms as the novel’s true hero.
bg: Victor Hugo published the novel in 1831 as Notre-Dame de Paris. It became so popular that it helped prompt the cathedral’s nineteenth-century restoration and the wider preservation of Gothic architecture in France. Interest in it surged again after the 2019 fire at Notre-Dame.
br: Hugo includes long chapters on architecture and the city, especially A Bird’s-Eye View of Paris; read them for atmosphere, or skim and return later. The story is far darker than film adaptations suggest.
la: Hugo mixes melodrama, grotesque comedy, historical detail and essayistic digression, contrasting beauty and ugliness, spirit and flesh, in a deliberately Romantic style. Characters are larger than life, and Hugo openly addresses the reader with opinions and lessons.
cx: Written partly to defend Gothic architecture against neglect and demolition, the novel also reflects post-revolutionary questions about the Church, justice and the people of Paris. Its chapter This Will Kill That argues that printing replaced architecture as humanity’s book.
th: Beauty and monstrosity
Outward ugliness can hide a loving heart, and beauty can hide emptiness.
Obsession
Frollo’s forbidden desire slowly curdles into hatred and destruction.
Architecture and history
The cathedral embodies the memory of a whole people.
fit: Pairs with Les Misérables on your list and gives a fuller picture of Hugo.
mis: Long digressions on architecture and a grim ending may deter readers expecting a romance.
rq: What role does the cathedral play?
How does Hugo make Quasimodo sympathetic?
dq: Why does Hugo care so much about buildings?

sum: Meursault, a French office clerk in colonial Algiers, attends his mother’s funeral without showing grief, begins an affair the next day, and drifts into the company of a violent neighbour. On a blazing beach, he shoots an Arab man for no clear reason. His trial becomes less about the killing than about his refusal to feel or perform the emotions society expects.
bg: Albert Camus published the novel in 1942, the same year as The Myth of Sisyphus, which explains his philosophy of the absurd. Camus won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1957 and died in a car accident in 1960.
br: Very short; read it in a day or two. Pay attention to the flat, plain style of Part One and how the second part, in prison and at trial, changes it.
la: Camus uses a detached first-person narrator who reports sensations rather than feelings, creating an uncanny effect, while light and heat dominate the imagery. Short declarative sentences mirror Meursault’s refusal to interpret his own life.
cx: Set in French Algeria, the novel has been criticised for leaving the murdered Arab man unnamed; Kamel Daoud’s 2013 novel The Meursault Investigation retells the story from his brother’s perspective.
th: The absurd
Life has no meaning beyond what we experience, and society cannot accept that.
Honesty and conformity
Meursault is condemned for refusing to perform emotions.
Colonialism
The nameless victim reveals the colonial world’s blind spots.
fit: Pairs directly with The Myth of Sisyphus already on your list, and with the existentialist titles.
mis: Meursault’s detachment can feel alienating, and the colonial framing is troubling. Some readers find it cold.
rq: Why does Meursault shoot the man?
What is he really on trial for?
How does his view change in prison?
dq: Is Meursault a hero, a monster or neither?
How should we read the unnamed victim today?

sum: In the Algerian coastal city of Oran, rats begin to die in the streets, and soon people do too. As plague spreads and the city is sealed off, Dr Bernard Rieux and a handful of others, a journalist trapped far from his lover, a civil servant writing a novel, a priest and a stranger organising volunteers, respond in different ways to an indifferent catastrophe.
bg: Albert Camus published the novel in 1947. It is widely read as an allegory of the Nazi occupation of France and the Resistance, in which Camus took part, and it found millions of new readers during the COVID-19 pandemic.
br: The narrator’s identity is revealed only near the end; notice the measured, chronicle-like voice. The book is slower and more reflective than The Stranger. Its five parts follow the epidemic’s course.
la: Camus writes as a sober chronicler, avoiding heroics; the ensemble of characters lets him explore different philosophical responses to suffering. Long conversations, such as Tarrou’s confession, carry the book’s ideas without becoming lectures.
cx: Written in the aftermath of the Second World War, the novel expresses Camus’ ethic of solidarity and decency in the face of the absurd. Oran itself had cholera outbreaks in the nineteenth century.
th: Solidarity
Ordinary decency and shared work are the best response to suffering.
Faith and suffering
The priest struggles to explain the death of innocents.
Exile and separation
Quarantine separates lovers, families and whole communities from each other.
fit: Pairs with The Stranger and The Myth of Sisyphus, and with Exhalation’s thought experiments on facing the inevitable.
mis: Its slow, reflective pace and allegorical distance may feel dry to some readers.
cw: Epidemic disease and death, including the death of a child.
rq: How do different characters respond to the plague?
Why is the narrator so restrained?
What does Rieux mean by decency?
dq: Is the plague an allegory, a real event, or both?
How does the novel read after a real pandemic?
